beur-hagra/1:א: (א) Seif 1 — one who does, etc. See Tosafot 50a s.v. "a place," etc., and proof from what is written above 308:1 "let us say," etc., and Tosafot there s.v. "let us say," etc., and Tosafot Eruvin 5:2 s.v. "and the Mishnah."
beur-hagra/1:ב: (ב) And even — as on Chol HaMoed; see siman 472 seif 1 and as written below.
beur-hagra/1:ג: (ג) And there is one who forbids, etc. — as on Chol HaMoed; see Moed Katan 12:1 and letter 4 of Pesachim and Moed Katan 13:1: erev Pesach equals Chol HaMoed only in those matters the Sages distinguished; and though on erev Pesach prohibition is only rabbinic, nevertheless amira l'akum is forbidden in rabbinic matters too, as in the case of a non-Jew coming to extinguish, etc., and even if he did it himself it is forbidden as in the case of a non-Jew who brought flutes, etc., and they said one who comes from outside the boundary, etc.; and further Chol HaMoed some say is rabbinic.
beur-hagra/1:ד: (ד) And there is, etc. — as in Bava Metzia 90a: they asked — it appears in rabbinic prohibition it is plainly permitted, and though on Shabbat forbidden even in rabbinic matters as above, Shabbat is different since its essence is d'oraisa as Tosafot wrote in many places; Chol HaMoed is not proof as Tosafot there s.v. "but," etc. Per the first reasoning one may say the same on erev Pesach, for it too is included in moed; and further one may say in every melacha prohibition they decreed lest it lead to Shabbat.
beur-hagra/4:א: (א) Seif 4 — one who travels, etc. All Rambam's language; see Tosafot there 51a s.v. "Rabbah," etc., and he holds the sugya in Chullin is displaced before Pesachim and the Mishnah deals with one who does not intend to return; and what R' Zeira ate was because he disputes R' Yosef as explained "who said this," etc.; see Tosafot there s.v. "Yosef," etc. But per Pesachim's conclusion it must be as Yerushalmi brought and Rosh brought there: any stringency due to error need not be practiced as stringencies of the place; R' Zeira held it was error as explained there; thus "one who travels," etc., and "similarly one," etc. — letter 40 at first deals with one who does not intend to return; see responsum Rashba siman 357 and his view on this.
beur-hagra/4:ב: (ב) He should not do — there 52a, and he holds one who does not intend to return — unlike Tosafot there.
beur-hagra/4:ג: (ג) And one who travels, etc., and we impose, etc. — Mishnah there.
beur-hagra/4:ד: (ד) And nevertheless, etc., forever — there 51b; Rava explained: unlike appearing before them; the Mishnah means: forever one should not change, etc., meaning he should not appear before them — thus "and nevertheless," etc., forever, etc.
beur-hagra/4:ו: (ו) And provided — there: since they saw him fasting; and though Abaye objected, this is because it is discreet and they already found him eating — no dispute among scholars, for scholars know he acted lawfully — see there in Ran. Tosafot's view there and in Chullin explains the first answer and Rosh in chapter 4 of Pesachim that the Mishnah teaches separately and everything after intending to settle — whether stringent as in the Mishnah or lenient as in the two cases — nevertheless one should not change before them even to be stringent as the Mishnah states specifically because they say how many, etc. — otherwise he must act like them since there is no Torah prohibition; see Tosafot there 52a s.v. "from a place," etc., and the case in settlement is forbidden, etc., with intention to return — if without intention to return, once he reached settlement even in wilderness forbidden, for everything follows the place he intends to settle; even if he left from there as explained in Sefer 496:3 sons of Israel, etc., per Tosafot as above; all this not from the Chullin case; but if: as above everything follows where he intends to settle; and all, etc., from the Chullin case as above.
beur-hagra/5:א: (א) Seif 5 — even, etc. Rambam's language; he holds the Mishnah where they practiced to do deals with it; he explains the Sages are lenient from R' Meir and do not dispute to forbid; so Ra'avad there from what is difficult; and the Sages only do three crafts, etc., as explained in the Gemara there "come hear R' Meir," etc., "and they work," etc. — meaning they finish only where they practiced to do; thus "a place where they practiced not," etc., specifically for Festival need as in the Gemara there; see Levushei Serad; and the three crafts specifically for Festival need as in Moed Katan 13:1; he ruled like the Sages and R' Meir only in the three crafts.
beur-hagra/5:ב: (ב) And there are those lenient — explaining the Mishnah where they practiced not to do; in the Gemara "and they work," etc., means even not for Festival need; thus in the Gemara "a place where they practiced not," etc., "for Festival need," etc. — two proofs that not for Festival need — per Rambam what he wrote "a place where they practiced not" cannot be explained; the question remains.
beur-hagra/5:ג: (ג) Three, etc. — specifically for Festival need; he need not have written "for Festival need" as Moed Katan 13:1; so Ra'avad in objections and Tosefta: "a place where they practiced melacha on erev Pesach," etc., "even where they said not to do, the three crafts they do — tailors," etc.
beur-hagra/5:ד: (ד) And if he began, etc. — meaning where they practiced not to do; he relied on the beginning and also "until midday" was only to exclude what Rosh wrote in the name of R' Yehuda that all day is permitted.
beur-hagra/6:_: Seif 6 — that is, etc. Magen Mishneh for the Aruch's version.
beur-hagra/7:_: Seif 7 — hen, etc. Rambam's text begins on Chol HaMoed; the question from "if it died," etc., see siman 476 seif 4 — meaning what R' Huna said "within three" refers to the beginning and on Chol HaMoed; after three days of sitting refers to the end; second view — and one who examines Rambam will see his intent is not so, for he did not mention "within three days for rebellion" at all; Maharif omitted R' Huna's words but ruled like Rav Ami and Rambam like R' Huna.
beur-hagra/9:א: (א) Seif 9 — the dung, etc. Per Rif's view it applies also on the fourteenth unless R' Chananel's text as explained; Rambam omitted it and only wrote regarding Chol HaMoed; Beit Yosef wondered — it is simple the Gemara text is read as ours and Abaye: both are on Chol HaMoed, etc.
beur-hagra/9:ב: (ב) Seif 14 — and they practiced — Shabbat 129; he wrote "and they practiced" to exclude Rif who wrote since many tread on it, etc., and in my humble opinion.
chok-yaakov/1:א: (א) From midday onwards. The reason is in the Yerushalmi: since it is the time of offering sacrifice, and when an individual brings a sacrifice melacha is forbidden (unlike the tamid which is a communal sacrifice — and understand not like Ateret Zekenim); and even nowadays when there is no sacrifice the prohibition remains in place, as the reason is explained in the Rosh and Ran chapter Kol Sha'ah. This reason was adopted by all Poskim; however Rashi wrote another reason at the beginning of chapter "the place where they practiced" — that one should not be preoccupied with melacha and forget removal of chametz, slaughtering the Pesach, and preparing matzah from beforehand, end of his words (and what Magen Mishneh wonders on Rashi — see Netsiv and Levushei Serad and Taz). A practical difference between the reasons: according to Rashi, if erev Pesach falls on Shabbat, melacha is forbidden on erev Shabbat from midday onwards since then is the time of removal and preparing matzah; unlike other Poskim whose reason is the sacrifice — then since the Pesach sacrifice overrides Shabbat, melacha is permitted on erev Shabbat until minchah as above siman 251; and so Maharil in laws of Shabbat Hagadol. And it appears to me there is no dispute at all in the reason, for certainly Rashi too was not unaware of the Yerushalmi — rather Rashi explained explicitly the reason where they practiced prohibition all day; but that from midday we excommunicate is necessarily from the Yerushalmi reason — therefore we excommunicate one who does melacha; understand well.
chok-yaakov/1:ב: (ב) We excommunicate him. Rambam chapter 7 of laws of Yom Tov wrote: and all the more so one strikes him lashes of rebellion; Magen Mishneh wrote the reason that excommunication is more severe than rebuke, as explained in chapter 1; and so Tosafot in Kesubos daf 28 and in Rashi Kiddushin daf 70b; and see Orach Chayyim siman 26, 119, 134 and Ba'er Sheva and responsum Sha'ar Efrayim siman 64.
chok-yaakov/1:ג: (ג) We excommunicate him. The implication of the Gemara and Poskim is also that he does not see a sign of blessing forever — meaning what he profits from the melacha he loses from another place; specifically on erev Pesach, unlike other eves of Festivals and erev Shabbat where one who does melacha from minchah onwards does not see a sign of blessing but we do not excommunicate him, only that doing it is forbidden as in Rambam chapter 8 of laws of Yom Tov; and so in Shulchan Aruch; and so is clear explicitly in the sugya beginning of chapter "the place where they practiced" — this is simple and clear, unlike Taz in Yoreh De'ah siman 70 who understood that since we do not excommunicate him there is no prohibition — therefore he wonders there on Beit Yosef; but in truth there is no difficulty. And what Taz further wonders in Orach Chayyim siman 485 and in Shulchan Aruch siman 7 regarding Beit Yosef's words contradicting each other — in Yoreh De'ah siman 70 he wrote one who sells a Torah scroll does not see blessing in them, implying that if there were any prohibition it would not say "there is no sign of blessing" implying there is no prohibition; and in siman 485 regarding the four perutot — he left it requiring further study. In my humble opinion there is no difficulty: certainly regarding the four perutot it must be there is no sign of blessing but no prohibition; and know that taking wages for writing Torah scrolls — why is it listed? Because twenty-four fasts the men of the Great Assembly sat on Torah scribes lest they grow wealthy, for if they grow wealthy they will not write again — therefore it is permitted to take wages, otherwise they would still refrain since taking wages is forbidden; understand well. And since he included them all in one passage saying "there is no sign of blessing," it implies there is no prohibition in any of them; and similarly one who takes orphans' money for wages listed there certainly has no prohibition at all. It is also possible this is Beit Yosef's intent: since regarding the four perutot he says "there is no sign of blessing" implying in the coins themselves there is no blessing, and he does not also say "does not see sign of blessing" as regarding selling a Torah scroll where it implies regarding the person engaged in it that he commits a prohibition — understand well. Thus Beit Yosef's words are correct without doubt.
chok-yaakov/1:ד: (ד) And so is the custom Maharshal wrote they get haircuts after midday through akum but not through a Jew. Magen Avraham in seif katan 3 wrote scribes too — even through akum it is forbidden to shave after midday (Magen Tzedek); and it appears the reason is tilting the head and assisting somewhat, end of his words. And there is no reason in this at all, for if he can cut his own hair he is permitted, as included in "he repairs his utensils for Yom Tov" as in responsum of R' Yosef Minz siman 4; even if the ink is not clear, repair alone is permitted unlike complete melacha as Beit Yosef explained Ra'avyah and as Mechaber and Rav in the gloss seif 2; and R' Yosef Minz must explain Ra'avyah that even complete melacha for one's own Yom Tov need is permitted, as Netsiv and Levushei Serad explained Beit Yosef; nevertheless in haircutting that tilts the head and assists somewhat this is certainly not complete melacha and assisting has no substance — permitted according to all. Mahariv and Maharil wrote cutting nails is forbidden after midday; Ateret Zekenim permits cutting nails if one forgot before midday. Law of mourner whose mourning fell in the middle of erev Pesach — see Yoreh De'ah siman 399. Magen Avraham wrote everything permitted on Chol HaMoed is all the more so on erev Pesach.
chok-yaakov/2:_: His utensils for Yom Tov. See siman 251 in Beit Yosef — it is clear the law permits repairing for others for free when it is not complete melacha; writing for others even for free is forbidden — see there.
chok-yaakov/3:א: (א) Not to do — they do not do. And since they practice thus as a fence and safeguard as Magen Avraham wrote above seif katan 1, it applies to them and their descendants and those who come to dwell there, as explained explicitly in Yoreh De'ah siman 214; and what Magen Avraham wrote here are simple matters explained there explicitly.
chok-yaakov/3:ב: (ב) They do not do — and at night it is permitted — Gemara.
chok-yaakov/3:ג: (ג) And for us, a place where they practiced not to do — the Levush wrote he did not see they practiced prohibition, end of his words.
chok-yaakov/4:_: One who travels from a place where they do. I already wrote this general rule in my book Ma'aseh Yehoshua general rule 98 seif 7 and made supports for Shach's words in Yoreh De'ah siman 214 and challenged Netsiv there — see there that they did not understand thus; and now I saw Magen Avraham also left Shach's words in Yoreh De'ah siman 14 requiring further study and mixed the views together; to clarify the matter I needed to clarify the views and the reason for the dispute. This entire seif the Mechaber copied is literally Rambam's language chapter 8 of laws of Yom Tov. From his language in "and similarly one whose intention is to return," etc. — the beginning of the matter deals with one who does not intend to return; and he holds one who travels from a place where they do to a place where they do not should not do melacha only because of dispute, specifically even if he wants to do discreetly — nevertheless since his intention is to settle there we fear lest they notice once that he does and come to dispute (however if his intention is to return, discreet practice is permitted since he is there incidentally — we do not fear dispute). However in the wilderness we do not fear dispute and he may do even if he does not intend to return — so Magen Mishneh, this is Rambam's view; and there are disputants, specifically outside the city's boundary as in the Gemara Chullin daf 110a. Regarding stringencies of the place he left — even without intention to return he must practice stringencies of the place he left, unlike the implication of the sugya first chapter of Chullin; and it is possible he holds the sugya in chapter "the place where they practiced" disputes that of R' Zeira and he does not hold like Tosafot that they teach separately — all this per Rambam's view. His reason: the main custom applies to the person from the place he left; stringencies of the place he went to are only because of dispute as stated. However per Rosh and Ran in chapter "the place where they practiced" and Rivash siman 44 — each city accepts its custom upon itself and all attached to it; and "we impose stringencies of the place he left" applies when his intention is to return; but if he does not intend to return he must keep the custom of the place he went to even discreetly — he may not do even in the wilderness since the custom of where he is now applies by law, not because of dispute. However if he has not yet reached the city's boundary once, he is not obligated to practice their custom — so Kolbo in laws of Pesach in the name of Torat HaMinhagim; and if his intention is to return he is not obligated by law to practice stringencies of the place he went to, only because of dispute he should be stringent publicly and discreetly permitted in everything except melacha which is conspicuous — forbidden discreetly in the city. All this is simple and clear for one who examines their words well. The Mechaber who copied Rambam's language appears he ruled like him, and so appears from his words below siman 496 (though Acharonim differ on several points — see there). In Yoreh De'ah siman 214 and below siman 474 he ruled like Rosh, Tur, and Ran; on this Shach in Yoreh De'ah siman 214 wonders that unlike Acharonim he mixed views, and in Rambam's language the Mechaber copied here they explained like Rosh and supporters and did not analyze this, for it is impossible to reconcile entirely; see responsum Radbaz part 1 siman 73 brought in Shulchan Aruch — also clear there are differing views among Poskim; requires further study there and in responsum Rashba siman 337. What Shach distinguishes between intending to return or to settle permanently — Kolbo in laws of Pesach in Torat HaMinhagim similarly distinguishes: regarding leniencies of the place he left — if he does not intend to return immediately, even if he intends to return later; but stringencies of the place he left he practices as long as his intention is to return forever, end of his words. For practical law Shach there agrees with Rosh, Tur, and Ran, and so appears among Acharonim, except they did not notice all this dispute I wrote. See Magen Avraham in the name of Maharil regarding youths who study — considered intending to return and must practice stringencies of the place they left; see there regarding leniency of lung examination and regarding eating Rhenish patzikan — see there. I was asked by people of the community of Vienna: before the expulsion there was a custom to forbid patzikan; now that community was dispersed and Ashkenazim settled there whose custom is to eat patzikan in their country — are they obligated to practice stringencies of the place they went to, or do we say since the community was nullified and dispersed their custom ceased? I answered: plainly per Rambam the main custom applies to the person from the place he left, whether lenient or stringent — only because of dispute must he practice stringencies of the place he went to; plainly they are permitted, for there is no dispute at all. Even per other Poskim I wrote, still there is no general rule here since the community was nullified their custom ceased and the original act removed — new faces came here; needless to expand on this fixed stake already expanded in Sha'ar Efrayim siman 70 and responsum Maharam Alshikh siman 68 and Tzemach Tzedek siman 16 — for even sanctity of the Land we hold first sanctity sanctified for its time and not for the future; see Yoreh De'ah siman 331. And if people of that city themselves resettled where they are lenient, they may eat — we do not impose stringencies of the place they left per these Poskim; though I saw in Magen Avraham below siman 493 in the name of Shach he doubts in similar cases — in my humble opinion there is no doubt at all and doubt does not remove certainty; and even if Shach's words can be explained another way — I did not see Shach's words themselves, requires further study there; but the law is clear as I wrote.
chok-yaakov/5:א: (א) And there are those who are lenient. Per this view, where they practiced to do, one may begin and finish on the fourteenth until midday in every matter; and so in Yoreh De'ah in the name of Ran; and so Kol Bo — obvious per Rosh since the Mishnah "one should not begin" deals where they do not do, but where they do one may begin every matter until midday; and the Rav omitted all this per his view as he wrote above seif 3 "for us where they practiced not to do" — therefore this is unnecessary; see above seif katan 7. See Kol Bo in laws of Pesach that shoemakers are also among the three crafts; so Rokeach siman 269 — requires further study how he ruled like R' Yosi and not like the Sages, for all Poskim ruled thus; also in Sefer Tzidah LaDerekh article 4 general rule 3 he omitted scribes and wrote shoemakers — requires further study.
chok-yaakov/5:ב: (ב) And it is for Festival need. See Shulchan Aruch that he derived from the sugya in Moed Katan chapter "one who overturned" that if he has nothing to eat he may do melacha even after midday — there is no greater Festival need than this; see what I wrote above seif katan 4.
chok-yaakov/6:_: That is, to prepare. It implies but to set initially on eggs is forbidden — so Taz and Magen Avraham, unless in the case mentioned in the next seif; and so Magen Mishneh end of laws of Yom Tov for one explanation of Rambam; however he concludes Rambam also agrees to Rashi that initially setting on eggs on erev Pesach is permitted (see Taz end of chapter "the place where they practiced"); and so Levush permits setting on eggs initially. See Tur and Beit Yosef that all these permitted matters are permitted all day even after midday, and similarly even where they practiced not to do — all day one may begin these melachos on the fourteenth — see siman 476.
chok-yaakov/8:_: One sweeps dung. Rambam's language: and they throw it outside to the garbage dump; and so is obvious in the Mishnah there, chapter "the place where they practiced" and on the Festival one moves it to the sides — see there.
chok-yaakov/9:_: And if it accumulated in the courtyard one takes it to the garbage dump. All this is Tur's language; below siman 475 he wrote if it accumulated until the courtyard became like a cattle pen they take it to the garbage dump; here he wrote simply "if it accumulated" implying he holds the fourteenth is lighter than Chol HaMoed. Rava's answer in the Gemara there daf 55b on the difficulty: you said dung one moves to the sides, then it teaches in a pen and courtyard one takes to the garbage dump — Abaye said there is no difficulty: here on the fourteenth, here on Chol HaMoed; Rava said both are on Chol HaMoed and it means: if the courtyard became like a cattle pen one takes to the garbage dump. Since Rava did not answer simply even on the fourteenth, certainly his intent is specifically on Chol HaMoed one does not take out unless the courtyard became like a cattle pen, unlike the fourteenth where any accumulation one takes out — nevertheless some accumulation is required from the rationale one should not take it out for free. Tur explained Rosh's words (though Rosh's words are obscure) as in the abridged rulings of Rosh: dung in the courtyard on the fourteenth one moves to the sides; if much dung accumulated in the courtyard one takes to the garbage dump; on Chol HaMoed one does not take out but moves to the sides, end of his words — clear as I wrote; all this appears simple to me. But I saw in Bach that he understood per Rosh and Tur the fourteenth and Chol HaMoed share the same law, and "if it accumulated" here also means until it became like a cattle pen; and he greatly strained to reconcile the sugya with them and that they dispute Rambam — see his words at length. Certainly the abridged rulings of Rosh I wrote escaped him — clear there is a difference between fourteenth and Chol HaMoed as Tur's language here and below siman 475; his words are correct per the sugya as I wrote; Beit Yosef too did not notice all this — in truth these matters are simple and clear for one who examines; there is no dispute among Poskim.
chok-yaakov/10:א: (א) Not to let blood. And similarly Kaporos that we call Kaporos (Mahariv and Maharil permit except on Hoshana Rabbah because it is a day of judgment), end of his words Magen Avraham; and it appears in any event on erev Shavuos one should be stringent, for the danger is greater as in chapter 18 of Shabbos, unlike other Festivals which are only a general decree because of erev Shavuos.
chok-yaakov/10:ב: (ב) On any Festival — Magen Avraham wrote in the name of Magen Tzedek: on the night before Yom Tov it is permitted to let blood except the night of Hoshana Rabbah. And on the last eve of Yom Tov of Pesach everything is permitted because it is not a Festival in its own right, end of his words.
peri-megadim/1:_: We excommunicate — Taz and similarly Magen Avraham letter 2 and Peri Chadash; Yoreh De'ah 334:62 and 86; and similarly a Torah scholar — we only strike discreetly; and nowadays one may say after midday is rabbinic; but in Temple times some say Torah prohibition after midday because of individual Pesach sacrifice, and some say rabbinic — see Peri Chadash proved from Pesachim 2:2 it is rabbinic on erev Shabbat; I did not understand whether they dispute before midday — custom or prohibition; on this Ra'avyah said: where do we find Sages forbade part from sunrise until midday and permitted until sunrise? The distance of two hours — here one does not err more than two hours; if so Magen Avraham will explain further.
peri-megadim/2:א: (א) And so Taz and Peri Chadash and Eshel Avraham siman 5:14 — all prohibitions forbid amira l'akum though not Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Chol HaMoed; Yoreh De'ah 297 and Shach letter 4 — must say specifically negative-commandment prohibition; positive-commandment prohibition permits amira l'akum in other prohibitions, unlike Yom Tov, Shabbat, and Chol HaMoed where even rabbinic matters forbid shevut through akum unless a mitzvah place — see Shulchan Gavoah 65 and 473:1 and Magen Avraham there and erev Pesach; even per those who say in Temple times perhaps forbidden because individual sacrifice is his Yom Tov — only positive commandment not negative. Responsum Maharam of Padua regarding Chol HaMoed whether negative or positive commandment regarding laying tefillin siman 108 and see siman 470 in Magen Avraham and if so explained there; and difficult from Shulchan Aruch 1 forbidding tooth extraction as capital offense and why permit here haircut and nails through akum; Ateret Zekenim 4 and 6 permitted if forgot before midday to cut after midday — requires further study; perhaps even nowadays after midday perhaps forbidden because of matter [prohibited] by vote, etc., like egg — Scripture implies perhaps Temple times — requires further study.
peri-megadim/2:ב: (ב) I was asked: one had fowl called capons walking in a garden and fears they will fly out — may he cut a small bone in the wing so they will not fly, or not? I answered: by himself it appears forbidden, for tza'ar ba'alei chayim without great need is forbidden — see siman 23:6 and siman 24 letter 8 in Shach there; through akum — if tza'ar ba'alei chayim is rabbinic, one may say amira in rabbinic matters in shevut of shevut in other prohibitions; perhaps permitted except Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Chol HaMoed as above and Peri Chadash; if tza'ar ba'alei chayim is d'oraisa forbidden — see Chayei Adam siman 272:9 implies tza'ar ba'alei chayim is rabbinic and see siman 75 letter 15 and therefore 13 from laws of murder and guarding life — if d'oraisa forbidden; if not, perhaps in other prohibitions amira l'akum is permitted and perhaps tza'ar ba'alei chayim is rabbinic — Maggid Mishneh laws of hiring 3 and Semag Choshen Mishpat 32 letter 12 they discuss regarding hiring workers — not resolved, see there; nevertheless one may say even if tza'ar ba'alei chayim is d'oraisa and has no negative commandment only positive, like erev Pesach after midday permitted through akum as stated; Ateret Zekenim 4 and Magen Avraham 3 — see there further.
peri-megadim/3:_: And for us — Taz and one who does not want to do melacha even where they practiced to do is permitted; an observer says he has no melacha — no arrogance and not because of dispute; where they practiced not to do — permitted at night until sunrise — Magen Avraham 5 — see there further.
peri-megadim/4:_: The tailors — Taz because we find leniency on Chol HaMoed; and if he has nothing to eat it is permitted even after midday — see siman 472:2; Chol HaMoed is stricter than erev Pesach after midday — Magen Avraham 3; in Peri Megadim laws of Yom Tov chapter 1 law 8; Ateret Zekenim 5; scribes means to shave — Magen Avraham 13; Ateret Zekenim 4 — those permitted to shave on Chol HaMoed, likewise erev Pesach after midday siman 471; giving garments to akum laundress after midday — for us where melacha through akum is permitted, this too — see there.
peri-megadim/5:_: That is — Taz: Mechaber ruled like Rambam on erev Pesach; Be'er HaGolah: to prepare a place, etc. — permitted all day even after midday; but to set on eggs forbidden after midday; where they practiced not to do — forbidden even before midday without having begun that day; and similarly if he began — only if for Festival need. But Tur explained like Rashi: setting means to hatch eggs, and similarly a hen that fled, etc.; Levush ruled like Tur and Rashi and Magen Avraham 14; this "to prepare a place" — if mere repair permitted; but to build them a coop, etc., one may say forbidden as complete melacha.
peri-megadim/6:_: And if — Taz; Beit Yosef's difficulty: it should have mentioned on the fourteenth after midday forbidden unless accumulated, etc.; Taz resolves: he only brings what the Gemara said and Rava establishes it on Chol HaMoed — see there; what is written here in seif 8 "one sweeps" means take outside; so in Mishnah Pesachim 55b — must say it deals when standing in the courtyard, unlike in a pen forbidden unless accumulated — on erev Pesach.
peri-megadim/7:א: (א) Not — Taz; last Yom Tov of Sukkot forbidden as a Festival in its own right — Magen Avraham 15.
peri-megadim/7:ב: (ב) It is impossible — psalm of thanksgiving on erev Pesach and Chol HaMoed of Pesach, etc., siman 429; in Peri Chadash there are places that practice saying it — correct not to say; accordingly if one began he does not stop; second view for Chayei Adam prayer — if he began obligatory prayer he stops for blessing in vain, unlike here finishing like saying Psalms and they say we in any event do not stop if he began; why need reason of chametz reducing eating time — matzah too one does not eat all day as siman 471 Magen Avraham 5 matzah of thanksgiving is not rich matzah; see Pesachim 13b: because of chametz reducing, etc. — strained to say it says perhaps and Aramaic 6:22 and 12:22; nevertheless some say its prohibition after midday is somewhat; for Rambam all day is difficult; one may say matzah of thanksgiving is a mitzvah — unlike coming to father-in-law's house before blessing, etc.; thanksgiving is a positive commandment unlike chametz reducing time; see Levush it is impossible and "to the conductor" impossible — erev Pesach last Yom Tov after midday Pesach sacrifice unlike other Festivals; see therefore Yom Tov atonement for sins all who eat, etc., and in my customs I wrote from this; see Yoreh De'ah 399:3 but on erev Pesach see there; one does not comfort a mourner on erev Pesach — Ateret Zekenim in the name of Rashi letter 20; see siman 478 and it implies all day even before midday one does not comfort on erev Pesach — requires further study; see Yoreh De'ah 399:8 near Beit HaBochir on erev Pesach and Shabbat; Shach letter 11 law of erev Pesach and Shabbat; see siman 464 in Magen Avraham; see there further erev Pesach when 13 Nissan falls, siman 494 — see there further.
